newsitem.title: CANADA: Floor trading ends at Toronto Stock Exchange.
newsitem.headline: Floor trading ends at Toronto Stock Exchange.

text.p: The Toronto Stock Exchange's closing bell sounded for the last time on Wednesday as the exchange closed its 30,000-square-foot trading floor and switched to computerized trading.
Ted England, head trader with Peters & Co. Ltd., made the ceremonial last floor trade, buying 100 shares of Bell Canada Enterprises Inc. from Donny Moss, a trader with RBC Dominion Securities.
Bell Canada first traded in 1905 and is considered Canada's pre-eminent blue chip stock.
The TSE, founded in 1861, is the world's seventh largest equities exchange, and the biggest in North America to relinquish its floor.
Closing the trading floor will save the TSE about C$4 million ($2.9 million) a year in real estate costs and result in efficiency gains, TSE Chief Executive Rowland Fleming said.

"To compete in the world arena, we must change and that is what we are doing today. We are witnessing a rite of passage that marks the beginning of a new era for the exchange and for Canada," Fleming told the traders, dignitaries and media who crowded the floor for the last trade.
The migration of stocks from the floor to Toronto's Computer Assisted Trading System began earlier this year.
Only a handful of traders remained on the floor in the last days before Wednesday's bell, down from a peak of 400 during the floor's heyday in the mid-1980s.
The remaining floor traders will join Toronto equity traders already working from their brokerage desks.
